source_text: Τί μοι λοπὸν καταλέγειν τὸ πλῆθος ὦν σέβονται ζώων Αἰγύπτιοι, ἑρπετῶν τε καὶ κτηνῶν καὶ θηρίων καὶ πετεινῶν καὶ ἐνύδρων νηκτῶν, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ποδόνιπτρα καὶ ἤχους αἰσχύνης; Εἰ δὲ καὶ Ἕλληνας εἴποις καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη, σέβονται λίθους καὶ ξύλα καὶ τὴν λοιπὴν ὕλην, ὡς ἔφθημεν εἰρηκέναι, ἀπεικονίσματα νεκρῶν ἀνθρώπων. Φειδίας μὲν γὰρ εὑρίσκεται ἐν Πείσῃ ποιῶν Ἠλείοις τὸν Ὀλύμπιον Δία, καὶ Ἀθηναίοις ἐν ἀκροπόλει τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν. Πεύσομαι δέ σου κἀγώ, ὦ ἄνθρωπε, πόσοι Ζῆνες εὑρίσκονται· Ζεὺς μὲν γὰρ ἐν πρώτοις προσαγορεύεται Ὀλύμπιος καὶ Ζεὺς Λατεάριος καὶ Ζεὺς Κάσιος καὶ Ζεὺς Κεραύνιος καὶ Ζεὺς Προπάτωρ καὶ Ζεὺς Παννύχιος καὶ Ζεὺς Πολιοῦχος καὶ Ζεὺς Καπετώλιος. Καὶ ὁ μὲν Ζεὺς παῖς Κρόνου, βασιλεὺς Κρητῶν γενόμενος, ἔχει τάφον ἐν Κρήτῃ· οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἴσως οὐδὲ ταφῆς κατηξιώθησαν. Εἰ δὲ καὶ εἴποις τὴν μητέρα τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν, μή μοι γένοιτο διὰ στόματος τὰς πράξεις αὐτῆς ἐξειπεῖν (ἀθέμιτον γὰρ ἡμῖν τὰ τοιαῦτα καὶ ὀνομάζειν), ἢ τῶν θεραπόντων αὐτῆς τὰς πράξεις ὑφ᾿ ὧν θεραπεύεται, ὁπόσα τε τέλη καὶ εἰσφορὰς παρέχει τῷ βασιλεῖ αὐτή τε καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτῆς. Οὐ γάρ εἰσιν θεοί, ἀλλὰ εἴδωλα, καθὼς προειρήκαμεν. ἔργα χειρῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ δαιμόνια ἀκάθαρτα. Γένοιντο δὲ τοιοῦτοι οἱ ποιοῦντες αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ ἐλπίζοντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς.
thought_title: Idolatry of the Egyptians and Greeks
pass_a_gloss: What to me is the benefit of recounting the multitude of things which Egyptians worship, of living things, and of reptiles and beasts and wild animals and birds and aquatic animals, and furthermore even footstools and shameful sounds? But if you were to tell also the Greeks and the other nations, they worship stones and wood and the rest of matter, as we have said before, images of dead men. For Phidias is found in Pisa making the Olympian Zeus for the people of Elis, and for the Athenians on the acropolis the Athena. I will ask you, man, how many Zeuses are found: for Zeus is called Olympian and Zeus of Latea and Zeus of Casius and Zeus of Ceraunius and Zeus the Forefather and Zeus the All-Night and Zeus the Guardian of the City and Zeus of the Capitol. And the Zeus who is the child of Cronus, having become king of the Cretans, has a tomb in Crete; but the others perhaps were not deemed worthy even of a tomb. But if you were to tell of the mother of the so-called gods, may it not happen to me to recount her deeds through my mouth (for it is unlawful for us to even name such things), or the deeds of her attendants by whom she is attended, as many as are the taxes and tributes which she and her sons provide to the king. For they are not gods, but idols, as we have said before. They are works of human hands and unclean demons. May those who make them and those who hope in them become such.
pass_b_english: Why should I bother recounting the countless things Egyptians worship—reptiles, beasts, wild animals, birds, aquatic creatures, even footbaths and shameful noises? If you turn to the Greeks and other nations, they worship stones, wood, and every kind of matter, mere images of dead men, as we have already said. Phidias, for instance, was found in Pisa making the Olympian Zeus for the Eleans, and the Athena on the Acropolis for the Athenians. Let me ask you, then: how many Zeuses are there? Zeus is called Olympian, Latean, Casius, Ceraunius, Forefather, All-Night, Guardian of the City, Capitoline. The Zeus who is Cronus’ son, once king of the Cretans, has a tomb in Crete; the others perhaps were not even deemed worthy of burial. If you mention the mother of the so-called gods, may I never have to recount her deeds (it is unlawful for us even to name them), or the deeds of her attendants who serve her, or the taxes and tributes she and her sons pay to the king. They are not gods but idols, as we have said—works of human hands and unclean demons. May those who make them and those who trust in them become like them.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex list of Zeus epithets and the parenthetical remark regarding the mother of the gods. Pass B's rendering of 'Γένοιντο δὲ τοιοῦτοι οἱ ποιοῦντες αὐτὰ καὶ οἱ ἐλπίζοντες ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς' as 'May those who make them and those who trust in them become like them' is a faithful interpretation of the optative expressing a wish/curse.

The Greek text is accurately translated in Pass A and Pass B. The title 'Idolatry of the Egyptians and Greeks' correctly reflects the content. All quoted clauses are properly cited with their corresponding source text. No omissions, additions, or distortions are present. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the distinctions between gods and idols, the worship of various deities, and the critique of idolatry. The parenthetical citations match the quoted content. The text is complete and faithful to the source.
